title: Module Variables, Functions and the __name__ Guard
learningObjectives: Explain module namespace and main guard and where it is useful in Python programs.
Choose correct Python syntax for module namespace and main guard.
Predict the result of representative PY16.7 operations.
Identify namespace, import and maintenance risks related to module namespace and main guard.
Apply module namespace and main guard in a small, readable Python program.

understand.concept: A module can define constants, functions and classes in its global namespace. Python sets `__name__` to the module's import name when imported, and to `__main__` when a file is run as the program's entry point. An `if __name__ == '__main__':` guard keeps demonstration or command-line code from running merely because another module imports the file.
understand.whyItMatters: The main guard allows one file to work both as an importable library and as a directly executable program.
understand.analogy: A module is like a labelled toolbox: related tools are stored together and another program can request the tools it needs.
understand.analogyLimit: A real Python module also has import rules, namespaces, execution behaviour and caching that a physical toolbox does not represent.
understand.summary: Module Variables, Functions and the __name__ Guard teaches how Python organizes and reuses related code.

explain.narrative:
## Names stored in a module
Functions, classes and variables defined at the top level become attributes of the module. Other code can access them with a qualified name after import.

## The __name__ variable
Python assigns a special `__name__` value. A module imported by another module normally receives its import name; the entry-point file receives `__main__`.

## Protect entry-point behaviour
Place command-line startup code inside `if __name__ == '__main__':`. Keep reusable functions outside the guard so they remain importable.

## Test the distinction
The examples simulate separate module namespaces with dictionaries and `exec`, making the two `__name__` values visible without creating project files.

examples.title: Read the current module name
examples.explanation: When the validator executes a lesson as a script, its main module name is __main__.

examples.title: Define module-level reusable names
examples.code:
course = 'Python'
def describe():
    return f'Learning {course}'
print(describe())
examples.explanation: Top-level variables and functions become names in the module namespace.

examples.title: Simulate importing a module namespace
examples.code:
namespace = {'__name__': 'score_tools'}
exec("LIMIT = 100\ndef clamp(value):\n    return min(value, LIMIT)", namespace)
print(namespace['__name__'])
print(namespace['clamp'](120))
examples.explanation: A module namespace stores its module name and definitions.

examples.title: Run entry-point code only for __main__
examples.explanation: The guard runs startup behaviour only when the module is the program entry point.

examples.title: Keep definitions separate from startup
examples.explanation: Reusable definitions remain available whether the file is imported or run directly.
